target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would broadly reduce scheduling barriers because private employers and schools would treat it as a non-working day
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to provide paid time off, so many retail and service workers would still work and low-income workers would still face barriers to voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would especially help low-income voters by reducing scheduling barriers
objection: Low-income workers are less able to absorb unpaid time off, so if private employers still schedule them, the holiday would not reliably remove the barrier and could disadvantage them.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is an effective turnout reform
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s broader argument that a national holiday is the best solution to work-schedule barriers
objection: State laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration are more direct and reliable ways to address turnout barriers than a federal holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that private-employer workers would still have to work on Election Day because federal holiday status does not require paid time off
objection: A national holiday typically changes real scheduling behavior beyond legal pay rules, including school closures and reduced hours or closures by many employers, so it would still reduce the need to miss work or class to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would not be helped by a holiday
objection: Low-income workers are the ones most constrained by the need to miss work or school, so reducing how often they must do so would especially help them.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday alone is not an effective turnout reform
objection: Holding elections on weekends or holidays is common across OECD countries, so holiday scheduling can work as a real voting-access practice and should not be presumed ineffective.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday-based election timing is practically workable because many OECD countries do it
objection: The fact that elections fall on weekends or holidays elsewhere does not show that low-wage workplaces close or that workers can take time off without losing pay or facing penalties, so it does not prove a U.S. holiday would remove barriers.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would reliably help low-income workers
objection: Without enforceable job-protected time off, private employers may still keep people working, so a holiday would not reliably reduce scheduling barriers for low-income workers.

target: AG1’s reliance on bipartisan support as evidence for the policy
objection: Public support shows popularity, not whether the policy will actually improve access or outperform other reforms.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not be worthwhile unless it eliminated every barrier for every subgroup
objection: A policy can still be justified if it meaningfully reduces major civic barriers and encourages participation, even if some private-employer workers still face costs.

target: AG2’s assumption that the holiday’s benefits are invalid because some workers may still face scheduling costs
objection: The civic-participation benefits of making voting a celebration still count even if the holiday does not perfectly eliminate every scheduling barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is not legitimate because it is only popular, not substantively justified
objection: Broad bipartisan support suggests the reform is democratically legitimate and valued across both major parties.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not reliably reduce work obligations because some private employers might still schedule work
objection: A nationally recognized holiday changes scheduling norms in practice by prompting schools and many employers to reduce or close operations, so it can make time away to vote more predictable.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would still face the same work barrier
objection: Because low-income workers are least able to absorb lost pay or unreliable scheduling, reducing work-obligation pressure would particularly help them.

target: AG1’s claim that a nationally recognized holiday creates a uniform non-working norm that meaningfully helps low-income workers
objection: Retail and service workplaces still commonly operate on holidays, especially for low-income workers, so the non-working norm is not uniform where it matters most.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would help low-income workers enough to count as a reliable voting-access reform
objection: If low-income workers still face holiday shifts or staffing requirements, the work barrier persists despite the holiday.

target: AG1’s reliance on OECD holiday/weekend election timing as evidence that the approach works in the U.S.
objection: Foreign election-day timing does not show that the U.S. holiday would be reliable for the low-income workers most affected by scheduling barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that OECD weekend/holiday elections do not prove anything about U.S. reliability
objection: The international pattern shows that weekend/holiday election timing is workable in real labor and school systems and therefore undermines the claim that a holiday election day would inherently fail.

target: AG2’s claim that the OECD and bipartisan evidence does not support the holiday approach
objection: If many comparable countries use weekend/holiday election timing and many Americans support it, it is not well-supported to call the reform inherently unreliable for low-income voters.

target: AG2’s claim that school closures do not help low-income parents/guardians enough to matter
objection: For many low-income families, weekday school status creates a real voting barrier because parents must supervise children or arrange costly coverage while voting; a holiday reduces that school-related cost.

target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a non-school day would meaningfully help low-income parents/guardians
objection: Even with schools closed, low-income parents still need supervision or childcare during polling hours and may still face work schedules, so the school closure does not reliably free them to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that the supervision/childcare issue defeats the holiday proposal
objection: The policy does not need to eliminate every constraint to be worthwhile; it is enough that it meaningfully reduces major scheduling burdens and increases voting feasibility for many.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not sufficiently help low-income parents/guardians
objection: Because a holiday also reduces work pressure while schools are closed, parents/guardians become more able to vote or arrange supervision without severe penalties.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday meaningfully helps low-income parents/guardians
objection: If the holiday does not reliably eliminate childcare/supervision needs or work penalties, then the combined barrier for low-income parents remains and they are still disadvantaged.

target: AG1’s broader justification that a holiday is worthwhile because it helps the most constrained group
objection: More reliable reforms exist—such as guaranteed time off for voting and automatic voter registration—so a holiday should be rejected if it cannot reliably remove the real barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday must eliminate every barrier to be justified
objection: A policy is justified if it meaningfully reduces major scheduling burdens and increases participation even when some barriers remain.

target: AG1’s claim that celebratory civic framing can make up for remaining barriers
objection: For low-income voters, the main constraint is practical ability to step away from work, so celebratory framing cannot by itself solve the access problem.

target: AG1’s assumption that a federal holiday gives workers the time off they need
objection: Federal holiday status does not legally require private employers to provide job-protected paid time off, so many low-income workers still would not have the needed time.

target: AG1’s use of turnout and civic-celebration benefits to justify the holiday
objection: If the key job-protected time-off constraint persists, the holiday is not an effective voting-access reform for the most affected group.

target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a holiday would improve access by shifting turnout to a day off
objection: A holiday can concentrate more people into the same in-person voting window, increasing wait times and overcrowding at polling places.

target: AG1’s claim that longer lines are not a reason to reject the holiday
objection: Long waits raise the time cost of voting and are more likely to deter low-income and shift-working voters who have less flexibility.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday necessarily creates overcrowding and long lines
objection: Because the holiday is predictable, election officials can plan staffing and capacity around the expected turnout, so long waits are not inevitable.

target: AG2’s claim that crowding would outweigh the holiday’s access benefits
objection: The main barrier for low-income voters is the ability to step away from work or school; reducing that barrier can still increase participation even if some locations are busier.

target: AG1’s claim that predictable holiday turnout can be planned for without major harm
objection: Actual turnout on Election Day is uncertain and election resources are fixed, so some polling places can still face more demand than planned and longer queues.

target: AG1’s claim that queue risk should not drive rejection of the holiday
objection: Long queues disproportionately deter voters who have the least flexibility, so even partial risk of congestion is a serious downside for low-income voters.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would create universal same-day crowding at polling places
objection: Because many voters can use early in-person or absentee/mail voting, a holiday does not force everyone into the same Election Day polling window.

target: AG2’s claim that queue risk is a reason to reject the holiday
objection: Since some voters can vote early or by mail, crowding at in-person polling places should not be expected to block low-income voting at large scale.

target: AG1’s claim that early voting and absentee/mail options reduce the need to worry about Election Day scheduling
objection: Those options require advance time, paperwork, or weekday voting, which low-income shift workers may also struggle to do, so they do not reliably remove the barrier.

target: AG1’s claim that Election Day is less important because other voting options exist
objection: For the most constrained voters, Election Day remains the critical opportunity, and a holiday does not guarantee job-protected time off on that day.

target: AG2’s claim that early/absentee options make a holiday unnecessary
objection: Many low-income schedule-constrained voters cannot reliably use those alternatives, so Election Day itself remains especially important for them.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday still does not solve voting access for the most constrained voters
objection: Making Election Day a non-working and non-school day reduces the day-of scheduling barriers that block many Americans from voting.

target: AG1’s claim that low-income voters who cannot use early or absentee voting will still benefit from a holiday
objection: Even then, they still need job-protected time away during Election Day hours, and a federal holiday does not guarantee that for private-employer workers.

target: AG1’s claim that reducing day-of barriers is enough to improve access
objection: If the holiday does not reliably create job-protected time off, then Election Day remains a barrier for the very voters the policy is meant to help.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday cannot help because it does not guarantee paid leave
objection: The key practical barrier is the amount of time workers must be away from work or school, and a holiday can reduce that required absence even without universal paid leave.

target: AG2’s claim that the absence of guaranteed leave makes the holiday ineffective
objection: A predictable holiday allows election administrators to adjust logistics, potentially shortening polling time and making voting easier even without mandatory paid leave.

target: AG1’s claim that shorter polling time makes the holiday effective
objection: Even shorter lines do not eliminate the risk of wage loss or discipline if workers still have to be absent during poll hours and employers are not required to protect that absence.

target: AG1’s claim that reducing time-at-poll is enough to improve access
objection: If workplace penalties still apply to any absence, then shorter in-poll time does not reliably translate into voting access for low-income workers.

target: AG2’s claim that short absences still leave workers exposed to penalties and therefore the holiday is ineffective
objection: Short absences are much more manageable than long ones, so reducing the time required to vote lowers the practical cost and penalty risk for low-income voters.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not meaningfully change the workplace-penalty problem
objection: Because the day becomes a recognized non-working/non-school day, voting logistics can often be handled in shorter windows rather than requiring a whole-day absence.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces wage-loss/discipline risk for low-income workers
objection: Federal holiday status still does not require private employers to provide job-protected paid time off, so low-income workers can still face wage loss or discipline even for partial absences.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would not increase time costs enough to matter
objection: Because more people would vote in the same window, polling-place capacity limits would likely raise wait times and time costs at least in some locations.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not reliably improve access because it does not guarantee protected time off
objection: When fewer people are scheduled to work or attend school on the holiday date, the practical amount of work or school time low-income voters must miss to vote is reduced.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday still leaves low-income workers with the same penalty risk
objection: Declaring Election Day a national holiday changes employer and supervisory expectations, reducing the chance that voting-related absence is treated as unauthorized.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is not reliable because private employers can still schedule workers
objection: Because the holiday is widely observed and predictable, the reduced penalty risk applies broadly and not just in isolated local practices.

target: AG2’s claim that wage-loss risk remains too high for low-income voters
objection: A national holiday means many workplaces and schools have fewer or no scheduled shifts, so workers need to miss less scheduled time to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not reliably reduce work/penalty costs
objection: By reducing the amount of scheduled work time that must be missed, the holiday meaningfully lowers wage-loss and discipline risks for many low-income voters.
